source.title: DGSAM: Domain Generalization via Individual Sharpness-Aware Minimization
source.authors: Y. Song; Youngsik Hwang; Jonghun Lee; Heechan Lee; Dong-Young Lim

record.file_problem: none; full paper and supplementary material are supplied.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own comparisons showing that reducing total-loss sharpness with SAM can leave individual source-domain losses sharp, and tests a domain-wise perturbation method against SAM on individual and unseen-domain sharpness. This refines the relationship between sharpness and generalization to domain shifts.
record.gate_note: The study reports model-level domain generalization accuracy comparisons, computational cost, domain-wise sharpness comparisons, and a perturbation-direction loss-increment comparison. Baseline accuracy rows are included where the table reports the compared results. Cited results from prior work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study uses the flat-minima generalization premise to develop DGSAM and evaluates domain-shift accuracy and unscaled loss sharpness. It does not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness ranking of training–test error gaps among similarly fitted networks, or any other listed version. Its total-versus-individual-domain sharpness argument concerns a different claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' conclusion: total-loss SAM can leave individual-domain losses sharp, while DGSAM reduces individual-domain sharpness, improves domain-generalization benchmark performance, and reduces overhead relative to SAM. The accuracy advantage is not universal: standalone DGSAM leads on three datasets and is described as comparable to SWAD on the other two.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates a domain-generalization optimizer using pretrained ResNet-50, Adam, and DomainBed leave-one-domain-out evaluation. Its outcomes concern out-of-distribution domain shifts rather than the listed in-distribution generalization claims.
record.method_sensitivity: DGSAM performance is evaluated across perturbation radii ρ on PACS and TerraIncognita; the paper reports it outperforms SAM across a wider range of ρ values.

fits_no_version.finding: Total-gradient perturbations increase some domain losses much more than others; sequential individual-domain perturbations produce more uniform increases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Domain-specific perturbation directions can expose loss sensitivity across source domains more uniformly than total-gradient directions.

fits_no_version.finding: Proposition 3.1 and the toy example show that ordering minima by total-loss sharpness need not order them by average individual-domain sharpness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Lower total-loss sharpness does not guarantee lower individual-domain sharpness.

fits_no_version.finding: DGSAM has lower reported source-domain, total, and unseen-domain zeroth-order sharpness than SAM; unseen-domain values are 42.46 versus 70.59.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Domain-wise gradual sharpness-aware training can reduce unscaled loss sharpness relative to SAM in the tested domain-generalization setting.

fits_no_version.finding: DGSAM achieves 88.5% mean target-domain accuracy on PACS, compared with cited ERM, SAGM, and SAM results of 85.5%, 86.6%, and 85.8%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: DGSAM improves PACS target-domain accuracy over these reported comparators under the DomainBed protocol.

fits_no_version.finding: DGSAM takes 0.169 seconds per iteration versus SAM's 0.217 on PACS with three source domains.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reusing domain gradients reduces DGSAM's per-iteration computational cost relative to SAM.

record.problems: The reported task is out-of-distribution domain generalization, separate from the claim's in-distribution held-out generalization. The sharpness comparison is reported for one dataset and the Table 2 text extraction flattens the domain columns. Main experiments use a pretrained ResNet-50 and report three repetitions; supplementary standard errors are referenced.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports extensive per-dataset, per-domain accuracy comparisons in Table 1 and supplementary Tables 4–8. They are not cataloged as claim-version rows because these domain-shift benchmark metrics do not test the listed in-distribution claims. Per-condition ρ sensitivity results in Figure 11 are described only qualitatively and likewise do not measure a listed version.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label accuracy, and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Width-dependent test error beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning regimes; using Adam throughout is not a comparison.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and changes to the training recipe.
Controlled dropout effects; searching dropout rates and reporting selected settings does not establish them.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, training–test error gaps at comparable training loss, and rankings against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts apply to V1–V8. The distinction from V7 rests on the sharpness definition and measured outcome, not solely on using different datasets. Table 1's caption describes its ± quantities as trial-based standard deviations, while other passages refer to standard errors; preserve that reporting ambiguity.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label held-out performance.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation on natural labels.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and tuning-dependent generalization.
Large-batch effects under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout effects on test error across training-set regimes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of train-test gaps.
Removal of memorized examples and resulting test accuracy.
